title: Mastering Ocular Surface Staining: The Clinician's Diagnostic Guide
summary: Ocular surface staining is the diagnostic cornerstone for evaluating tear film integrity, epithelial cell health, and corneal damage. This guide provides a systematic approach to interpreting vital dye patterns for precise clinical diagnosis.

sections.title: The Big Three Dyes: Comparative Utility
Red Flags for Cornea Specialists
content: Dendritic/Map-like staining: Consider Herpes Simplex Keratitis (HSV).
Punctate Epithelial Erosions (PEE) in 'catarrhal' configuration: Consider Staphylococcal hypersensitivity.
Rapid dye clearing: Possible aqueous leak (Seidel positive).
Confluent staining with stromal thinning: Impending corneal melt.

sections.title: Procedural Protocol
content: Step 1: Instill dye (use dry impregnated strips; avoid liquid solutions for infection control).
Step 2: Ensure adequate blinking to distribute the dye.
Step 4: Use Cobalt Blue filter (for Fluorescein) or White/Yellow filter (for Lissamine).
Step 5: Document size, density, and location using the NEI/Industry workshop grid.

content.explanation: S: Superior (SLK), T: Tear film (DES), A: Assessment (Systematic), I: Inferior (Exposure), N: Nature (Epithelial vs. Stromal).

sections.title: Clinical Pearls
content: Lissamine Green is the preferred dye for dry eye exams as it does not sting.
Always evaluate staining BEFORE tonometry to avoid false-positive abrasions.
Rose Bengal may mask underlying HSV; verify presence of dendrites first.
Staining patterns are dynamic; timing of assessment is critical.
